300.bp: This paper serves people who train models on records that arrive in time order: sensor readings, traffic measurements, health traces, energy loads, market signals, or any other stream where the past is used to forecast the future or classify the whole pattern. The central object is not just a clean sequence. It is a training set containing some examples whose future or label is hard to infer from the available history. Those examples may be noisy, may come from a rare situation, or may simply depart from the usual pattern in the data. If a training process treats every example as equally informative, the model can spend too much effort chasing cases that even a good rule cannot explain well. The paper asks a training-side question: before changing the forecasting or classification architecture, can the learning process notice which time-series samples are predictable enough to trust more, and which ones need a gentler penalty?
300.wh: The problem is hard because low predictability is not the same as ordinary error. Early in training, nearly every sample may look poorly handled because the model has not learned much yet. Later, a sample may still have high error because it is genuinely noisy, because it follows a rare pattern, or because the model itself is biased and has misjudged it. A simple training loss only sees the size of the mistake, not why the mistake happened. That makes the training loop unstable: examples that deviate from the normal data distribution can pull the model toward a poor set of settings, while easy examples may not get enough weight to form a reliable base. The abstract also says the method must work for both forecasting and classification, so the solution cannot depend on one narrow output type. It needs a general way to estimate predictability while the model is still changing.
300.naive: A smart beginner would train the time-series model with the usual error rule: predict the next values or the class, compare the answer with the target, and reduce all mistakes as much as possible. If some samples create large mistakes, the beginner might either punish them harder because they look important, or throw them away because they look like noise. Both choices are too blunt. Punishing every hard sample can make the model chase abnormal or low-predictability patterns and settle into poor training behavior. Dropping them can erase rare but legitimate cases. The paper's premise is that the training loop needs a middle position: focus first on high-predictability samples, but still learn from low-predictability ones in a controlled, staged way.
300.ap: The core idea is to make predictability part of the training rule itself. Instead of letting every sample's raw error speak with the same force, APTF tries to identify which samples appear low-predictability during training and changes how their penalty grows. Its Hierarchical Predictability-aware Loss dynamically separates samples by how predictable they seem and progressively expands the loss penalty for the low-predictability group as training evolves. In plain terms, the model first builds confidence from examples whose patterns are clearer, then gradually gives harder examples more influence rather than letting them dominate from the start. The second move is an amortization model. Here, amortization means using an additional learned estimator to spread the work of judging predictability across samples, so the system does not rely only on the current main model's possibly biased errors. That is meant to reduce mistaken predictability estimates caused by model bias.
300.mech: The mechanism begins with a batch of time-series training samples. Each sample is an ordered record, and the task is either to forecast future values or assign a class to the sequence. The main model produces an output for each sample. A loss function then measures how wrong the output is, but APTF does not stop at a flat penalty. It asks an extra question: given the sample and the current state of training, does this example look highly predictable, or does it look like a low-predictability case that may deviate from the normal data distribution? The Hierarchical Predictability-aware Loss uses that judgment to organize the penalty in levels. Clearer samples receive direct training pressure, while low-predictability samples receive a penalty that expands progressively as training proceeds. That schedule matters because an early model is not reliable enough to decide every hard case immediately. Alongside this, the amortization model estimates predictability in a way that is meant to reduce bias from the main model. If the main model is currently bad at a region of the data, raw error alone could falsely label those samples as intrinsically low-predictability. The amortization component supplies a separate learned estimate, and the resulting training signal tells the model what to emphasize now and what to learn from more cautiously later.
300.math: The main mathematical idea is a weighted training penalty. A training penalty is a rule that says how bad an answer is: a forecast far from the observed future is bad, and a wrong class assignment is bad. Ordinary learning repeatedly changes model settings to make that badness smaller. APTF changes the shape of the penalty by attaching it to predictability. Predictability is an estimate of how much useful pattern a sample seems to contain for the task, not a moral label saying the sample is worthless. The hierarchy means samples are not treated as one undivided pile; they are grouped by estimated difficulty or reliability, and the penalty for harder groups changes over training time. The progressive expansion is a curriculum-like choice: early updates lean more on cleaner evidence, later updates admit more difficult evidence. Probability enters as uncertainty about the sample itself: a high-error case might be noise, a rare valid pattern, or a place where the model is biased. The amortization model is a learned shortcut for estimating that hidden property across many samples, so predictability is not recomputed only as a raw consequence of the main model's current errors. The tradeoff is accuracy versus trust in the training data: use hard samples too aggressively and noise can steer the model; avoid them too much and rare patterns remain unlearned.
300.dots: This paper sits inside the time-series family because it treats ordered records as noisy streams whose future or class depends on reusable temporal structure. It connects to the sequence concept: the useful evidence is in the order and change of readings, but old, noisy, or abnormal stretches can blur what the sequence is saying. It also connects to probability, because the method must reason under uncertainty about whether a training example is informative or misleading. The learning-from-examples idea is central as well: the model is not given a hand-written rule for every domain, so it must reuse patterns from training samples while avoiding accidental noise. Finally, it links to choice-setting math, because HPL defines what counts as wrong and how strongly different samples should affect the search for better model settings. Compared with time-series papers that mainly change how histories are represented, this one changes how training evidence is trusted.
300.ww: The mechanism should help because training is path-dependent. Early updates can shape which patterns the model finds easy later. If low-predictability samples dominate those early updates, the model may spend its capacity explaining cases that do not reflect the normal data distribution, or it may move toward a poor local solution where later corrections are harder. By focusing first on high-predictability samples, the method lets the model learn a stable base pattern from clearer evidence. The progressive penalty then prevents a second failure: it does not permanently ignore hard samples. As training matures, low-predictability samples receive more structured pressure, so the model can still learn from rare or difficult cases when it has a better foundation. The amortization model helps because raw error is an unreliable judge of predictability. A biased main model can make a valid sample look hopeless. A separate estimator can smooth that judgment across cases, reducing the chance that the training rule confuses model weakness with sample uselessness.
300.po: The payoff is a general training framework for time-series forecasting and classification that addresses noisy, low-predictability samples directly. The abstract claims that APTF improves model performance from the training perspective rather than by proposing one new forecasting architecture. That matters because many deep learning models already exist for time series; a training rule that can sit across tasks may be useful when the data contains unstable or abnormal samples. The practical capability is more controlled learning: the model can emphasize clearer patterns while still learning appropriately from harder samples instead of letting them destabilize training or be discarded.
300.limits: The abstract does not prove that the method can reliably tell true noise from rare but important structure in every domain. It assumes that predictability can be estimated well enough during training to guide penalties, and that the amortization model reduces bias rather than adding a new one. The approach also depends on the staged penalty schedule being appropriate for the data and task. If low-predictability samples contain the main safety-critical events, delaying their influence could be risky. The abstract reports the design and intended effect, but not the domains, failure cases, sensitivity to schedule choices, or how much extra training cost the added estimator creates.

301.bp: A city service often needs to guess what will happen next: traffic demand, mobility flow, sensor readings, or another time-based quantity that changes hour by hour. The hard case is a target city with too little clean history. A forecasting model trained only on that city may not have seen enough mornings, weekends, disruptions, or seasonal shifts to learn dependable patterns. At the same time, other cities may have rich histories and useful documents describing past conditions. This paper serves the practical need to borrow that outside experience without pretending that every city behaves the same. Its object is not just a table of numbers, but a forecasting moment: the target city has a current situation, the source cities contain many possible past analogies, and the system must choose which outside cases are relevant enough to help predict the target.
301.wh: The central tension is that source-city data is both valuable and risky. If one city has many years of observations, it may contain examples of rush-hour buildup, holiday effects, weather-related changes, or platform demand patterns that a smaller city has not recorded often enough. But those examples are not automatically portable. Roads, commuting habits, sensing coverage, city size, and web service usage can differ, so a pattern that explains one city may be irrelevant or actively misleading in another. The abstract says existing transfer learning methods generally use all available source data without explicitly separating useful from non-useful knowledge. That is the failure point. More data can make the target model look better supplied while actually mixing helpful clues with noise. The difficult question is therefore not only how to forecast, but how to decide what outside history deserves to be heard.
301.naive: A smart beginner would gather every time-series record from the source cities, combine it with the small target-city record, and train one forecasting model on the merged pile. That beginner might reason that more examples should teach more patterns. The approach fails when the merged pile hides city-specific differences. If source and target distributions are not identical, the same time stamp, trend, or local event can mean different things in different places. The model may learn an average city that fits none of the cities well, or it may copy strong source-city regularities into a target city where they do not apply. In sparse data settings, the target city has too little evidence to correct those imported mistakes.
301.ap: The paper's core move is to put a selector in front of the forecasting engine. Instead of giving the model all source knowledge, xRAG4TS first searches for historical patterns and documents from data-rich cities that are semantically relevant to the current target-city forecasting case. Here, semantic relevance means that the outside case is judged similar in meaning or situation, not merely present in the same database. The chosen cases are then turned into structured prompts, which are organized pieces of text or data that tell a large language model what context to consider. The language model is used as an inference module: it receives the target-city situation plus selected source-city evidence and produces a forecast. The key idea is selective borrowing, where retrieval acts as a filter against harmful transfer.
301.mech: The mechanism begins with a target city that has sparse time-series evidence and a forecasting need. The input also includes richer source-city material: historical time-series patterns and related documents. First, the Cross-City Selective Retriever Module treats the current target case as a query. It compares that query with candidate source-city histories and documents, looking for cases that are close in meaning to the target situation. The abstract does not give the exact comparison formula, so the safe interpretation is that the retriever scores source material by relevance and filters out material judged non-useful. Second, the retained source evidence is reorganized into structured prompts. That matters because a language model does not simply absorb a database; it reads a bounded context. The prompt must therefore present the target situation, the retrieved historical patterns, and any useful documents in a form the model can use. Third, the LLM Inference Module reads this curated context and generates the forecast for the data-scarce target city. The output is a prediction guided by selected outside evidence rather than by blind transfer from the full source set. The visible trail of retrieved examples also gives a partial explanation of why the forecast was made.
301.math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath the paper. The first is similarity: the system needs a repeatable way to decide whether a source-city pattern is near enough to the target-city case to be useful. Closeness here is a compressed judgment. It must turn many details, such as temporal shape, city context, and document meaning, into a score that can sort candidates. The second idea is ranking. The retriever has a large pile of possible witnesses and must order them so the most relevant ones enter the prompt while weaker ones are ignored. The third idea is learning from examples across domains, often called transfer learning: patterns learned in one setting are reused in another, but only when the settings share enough structure. The fourth idea is sequence forecasting: ordered past values are used to estimate future values, because the next value depends partly on the path that led there. The forecast is therefore a judged continuation, not a detached label. The tradeoff is completeness versus contamination. Taking more source data may increase coverage, but selective retrieval tries to preserve useful signal while reducing misleading city-specific noise.
301.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of several recurring conference ideas. In the time-series and spatiotemporal family, it shares the pressure of forecasting from ordered signals whose meaning depends on place and time. In the retrieval-augmented generation family, it shares the question of which outside evidence should be fetched before a language model answers. In the similarity family, it depends on measuring which past cases are close enough to guide the present case. It also connects to transfer learning, where a model tries to borrow from a richer source domain without erasing local differences in the target domain. The broader pattern is selective context. Many 2026 systems are moving away from treating all available data as equally helpful. This paper makes that principle concrete for cross-city forecasting: source knowledge is useful only after the system has asked whether it actually matches the target city's current need.
301.ww: The approach can work because forecasting under scarcity is often an analogy problem. A target city may not have many local examples of a situation, but some source city may have faced a similar temporal pattern or documented condition before. If the retriever finds that case, the language model receives a smaller and cleaner set of clues than it would get from the full source archive. That reduces two common errors. First, it lowers distraction: irrelevant source patterns are less likely to dominate the prompt. Second, it lowers negative transfer, where a model imports a source-city rule that does not hold in the target city. The language model helps because it can read structured textual context and relate described situations, histories, and forecasting instructions. The decisive improvement is not that the model is large by itself; it is that the model is asked to reason over selected evidence. Selection turns outside data from a noisy flood into a set of candidate analogies.
301.po: The payoff is a more useful forecasting pipeline for cities that lack abundant high-quality data. Instead of waiting for years of local observations, a target city can use carefully chosen evidence from data-rich cities. The abstract emphasizes three practical gains: selective use of source knowledge, interpretability through the retrieved historical patterns and documents, and context-aware guidance for the language model. In ordinary terms, the system can say not only what it predicts, but which outside cases were brought in to help. That is valuable for urban mobility platforms and adaptive web-based decision systems where a forecast must be both useful and inspectable.
301.limits: The abstract does not provide the full retriever design, prompt format, datasets, evaluation numbers, or failure cases, so the mechanism can only be explained at the level it states. The method assumes that semantically relevant source-city cases exist and that the retriever can recognize them. If the target city is genuinely unlike the source cities, retrieval may return plausible but wrong analogies. The language model must also preserve numeric time-series structure well enough after it is expressed in prompts. Interpretability is partial: seeing retrieved cases helps, but it does not prove the model used them correctly or that the forecast will survive new sensing gaps, policy changes, or unusual events.

302.bp: LaTune serves the practical moment when a web application wants a language model response on a nearby device instead of a distant cloud server. The reason is concrete: local execution can keep user data closer to the user and can avoid network delay. But putting a large language model on an edge device is not just a question of choosing an inference engine. The engine has many runtime settings, and those settings decide how much memory is used, how much work is batched, how fast requests finish, and whether the device stays within its resource budget. A phone, small board, or local appliance is also not a stable machine: background apps, heat, memory pressure, and competing workloads can change what is affordable from one minute to the next. The paper is therefore about turning model serving into a live configuration problem: find settings that deliver useful throughput under changing resource limits without spending too much time searching.
302.wh: The hard part is that the best runtime configuration is a moving target. Edge devices have severe budget limits, so a setting that looks efficient on a roomy server may exceed memory, stall, or lose throughput locally. The device also changes over time because other processes contend for the same memory and compute. A simple fixed configuration assumes yesterday's resource picture still holds today, but the abstract says static methods fail under heavy contention. Searching is also expensive. Runtime settings form a large menu of possible combinations, and trying many of them costs exactly the scarce thing the system is trying to save: time on the device. The abstract points to three useful facts: some parameters matter more than others, tuning knowledge can transfer from past cases, and the ranking of good choices can stay stable enough to exploit. The difficulty is using those facts without pretending every device and workload is identical.
302.naive: A smart beginner would pick one of two direct approaches. The first is manual tuning: run a few tests on the edge device, choose the fastest configuration, and keep it. That fails when resource contention changes, because a configuration chosen in a quiet setting may become poor or infeasible when the device is busy. The second is exhaustive search: try every reasonable combination of runtime settings and keep the best measured one. That preserves completeness, but it wastes many trials on parameters that barely affect the outcome and on configurations already known to be unlikely from past evidence. On a small device, the tuning process itself becomes too costly, and the answer may arrive after the operating condition has changed.
302.ap: LaTune's central move is to treat runtime tuning as a selective, reusable, and adaptive search problem. Instead of treating every setting as equally important, it first focuses on the parameters that are most sensitive, meaning the ones whose changes actually move the performance and resource tradeoff. Instead of starting every device or model from zero, it transfers knowledge from historical tuning data when earlier cases are informative for the current case. Instead of producing one static setting, it uses a two-stage search process that can choose a configuration according to real-time resource constraints. In plain terms, LaTune narrows the menu, begins from prior experience, and then adjusts the final choice to the device's current budget. The abstract frames these parts as parameter selection, knowledge transfer, and two-stage optimization, all aimed at finding high-quality runtime configurations with few trials.
302.mech: The mechanism starts with an LLM inference workload on an edge device and a set of runtime configuration parameters. The inputs include the possible settings, measurements or historical records from earlier tuning runs, and the device's current resource condition. First, LaTune examines parameter sensitivity. A parameter is worth attention if changing it meaningfully changes the outcome, such as throughput or the balance among several objectives. Parameters that barely alter the result are less worth exploring, so the search space becomes smaller. Second, LaTune uses knowledge transfer. Historical data from related devices, models, or prior runs gives hints about where good configurations tend to be, so the new search does not spend early trials rediscovering obvious bad regions. Third, LaTune uses a two-stage selection process. One stage searches for promising candidates under the reduced and informed space; the other stage chooses among them according to the resource constraints visible at runtime. The configurations are compared by how well they trade off competing goals, reflected in the abstract's hypervolume result, and by throughput. The output is not a new language model. It is a chosen runtime configuration for running the existing model on the current edge condition.
302.math: The main mathematical idea is constrained search under changing budgets. Search means choosing among many possible settings; constrained means some choices are unacceptable because they exceed memory, time, or other resource limits. The paper's tuning problem also has more than one goal. Throughput should be high, but the configuration must remain feasible under device limits, and hypervolume is a way to summarize how much useful tradeoff space a method covers when several objectives matter at once. Parameter sensitivity is a ranking idea: measure which knobs change the result most, then spend search effort on those knobs. Knowledge transfer is a similarity idea: if previous tuning cases are close enough to the current device or workload, their measurements can guide the new search. Rank stability is an ordering idea: even if exact scores change, the relative order of good and bad configurations may stay similar enough to reuse. The tradeoff is accuracy of search versus tuning cost. LaTune accepts that it may not test everything, but it tries to skip work in places where evidence says the skipped choices are unlikely to change the final decision.
302.dots: In the repo's conference map, LaTune sits at the intersection of LLMs and efficiency. The LLM family is large in the current JSON data, with many papers asking how language models can be deployed, secured, adapted, or used in web systems. The efficiency and scalability family adds the shared pressure: useful systems cannot always afford the direct version of the computation. LaTune is a sibling to edge and deployment papers that save memory, latency, communication, or energy, but its object is not model weights or training data. Its object is the runtime configuration itself. It also connects to recommendation and retrieval work that ranks a small useful set from a large pile, because LaTune ranks and filters configuration choices. It connects to systems optimization papers because it defines a resource-aware objective and chooses settings under constraints. Its theme, LLM edge inference, makes privacy and latency practical pressures rather than abstract benefits.
302.ww: LaTune should work better than the naive approach because edge tuning has uneven structure. If all parameters mattered equally and every device behaved unrelatedly, then narrowing the search or reusing old measurements would be dangerous. The abstract says the opposite: parameter sensitivity, transferability, and rank stability provide exploitable structure. Focusing on sensitive parameters removes many low-value trials while preserving the knobs most likely to change throughput or feasibility. Transferring historical knowledge gives the new search a warm start, so early iterations test plausible regions instead of wandering through known weak choices. Rank stability matters because exact performance can shift across devices or contention levels, but the ordering of candidates may remain useful enough to guide selection. The two-stage process then handles the last local fact: the device's current resources. This is why the method can stay lightweight while adapting under heavy contention. It is not magic; it works because the configuration landscape is partly reusable and partly dynamic, and LaTune separates those two parts.
302.po: The payoff is faster and more reliable local LLM serving on constrained devices. The abstract reports experiments across four edge devices and LLMs. LaTune reaches up to 3.93 times higher hypervolume and up to 6.90 times throughput gains over baselines, which means it finds better operating tradeoffs and moves more inference work through the device. It also accelerates tuning by 2 to 3 times and converges within 10 to 20 iterations. In practical terms, developers get a way to tune runtime settings without long trial-and-error runs, and the system can keep executing under heavy contention where static configuration methods fail.
302.limits: The claims depend on the structure observed by the authors continuing to hold. Parameter selection helps only if a small subset of runtime settings really dominates performance. Knowledge transfer helps only if historical cases are similar enough to the current device, model, and workload. Rank stability helps only if good configurations remain good in roughly the same order when conditions change. The abstract reports four edge devices and LLMs, but it does not prove behavior on every hardware family, model size, inference engine, or workload mix. It also reports throughput and hypervolume gains, but the abstract does not detail the full quality, energy, thermal, or user-experience tradeoffs behind every selected configuration.

303.bp: This paper serves systems that answer questions such as: if one fact pattern holds in a knowledge graph, what matching fact should hold somewhere else? The graph stores entities as connected facts, but here each entity can also have text and images. That helps for ordinary objects: a picture can tell a system that a cat, chair, or building is the kind of thing being discussed. It is less helpful for abstract things such as actions or concepts, where a picture may be vague, decorative, or missing the point. The paper studies analogical reasoning in this setting: first infer the relation suggested by a source example, then complete the missing tail entity in a target example. Its central problem is not simply adding more media. It is deciding which source of evidence should be trusted for this particular analogy, and whether the inferred relation agrees with the pattern of media evidence implied by the context.
303.wh: The hard part is that the useful signal changes with the kind of entity and relation. A static merger of graph links, text, and pictures acts as if every source matters in the same way for every query. That assumption is too blunt. For concrete entities, images may expose visible properties that text leaves implicit. For abstract concepts and actions, the same images may add noise, while text descriptions and graph connections carry the decisive clue. Analogical reasoning makes this sharper because the system must perform two linked tasks. It first has to infer what relation is being expressed by the analogy, then use that inferred relation to find the missing tail. If the first step trusts the wrong media source, the second step starts from a bad relation. If the relation and the media pattern disagree, the answer can look plausible in one channel while being inconsistent with the analogy as a whole.
303.naive: A smart beginner would represent each entity by combining all available evidence: graph neighborhood, text, and image. Then they would use the same combined representation for every analogy, learn a relation from the source pair, and rank possible tail entities by closeness to the predicted answer. This fails because the mixture is fixed before the query is understood. It gives visual evidence the same status for a visible object as for an abstract action, even though the abstract case may need text and graph structure instead. It also does not check whether the relation just inferred is compatible with the kinds of evidence that should matter in this analogy.
303.ap: The paper's core idea is to make the evidence mixture relation-aware. RMAR uses two complementary paths. The explicit path builds a modality fingerprint, which is a compact description of which evidence sources seem relevant to the relation and analogical context. That fingerprint is used twice: to score whether a candidate induced relation fits the media pattern, and to guide how evidence is fused when predicting the missing tail. The implicit path uses adaptive gating, meaning it opens or closes the contribution of graph structure, text, and image according to the current query rather than by a fixed rule. The result is a reasoning process that can say, in effect, this analogy is mostly visual, or mostly textual and structural, before it commits to a relation and a tail entity.
303.mech: The input is a multimodal knowledge graph and an analogy query. The graph supplies entities and relations; the extra channels supply text and visual information for entities where available. The mechanism begins with relation induction. Given the analogical context, RMAR estimates a modality fingerprint: a pattern saying which channels should be informative for the relation being inferred. It then uses this explicit pattern to score compatibility, so a proposed relation is not judged only by whether its graph position looks reasonable, but also by whether the media evidence it depends on matches the context. Next comes tail completion. The system must choose the missing entity that best fits the induced relation. Here the fingerprint guides fusion, so the representation used to score candidates is not a single permanent blend. In parallel, the implicit path applies adaptive gates that condition the blend on the query itself. These gates weight structural, textual, and visual signals differently for each case. Candidate tails are then compared or scored under this query-specific mixture. The output is a ranked or selected tail completion that is tied to both the inferred relation and the modality pattern. The abstract also says RMAR is not tied to one backbone: it can sit on multimodal knowledge graph representation pipelines or transformer-based pipelines.
303.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing the work. The first is similarity: entities, relations, text, and images are turned into comparable descriptions so the system can ask which candidate tail is closest to what the analogy predicts. Closeness is useful because it turns a vague reasoning question into a scoring problem, but it is dangerous if the score hides the difference between visual, textual, and graph evidence. The second idea is weighting. Adaptive gating is a learned way to assign different weights to different evidence sources for each query. In plain terms, it is a set of controllable valves: let image evidence speak loudly for concrete entities, but quiet it when the relation points to an abstract concept. The third idea is consistency checking. A modality fingerprint acts like a small summary of the expected evidence pattern for a relation. It lets the system compare the induced relation against the channels that should support it. Finally, learning from examples adjusts these scores and gates so that repeated analogical cases teach the system which evidence sources were actually reliable. The main tradeoff is richer evidence versus noisy evidence: more channels help only when the model can decide when each channel should be trusted.
303.dots: This paper connects to the conference's knowledge-graph line because it treats facts as a network where links carry evidence about what other links may be missing. It also connects to multimodal vision-language work because the central question is how pictures and text should be aligned with structured facts. Its difference is the analogical setting: the task is not just link prediction, but relation induction followed by tail completion. Neighboring papers on multimodal recommendation and retrieval also face the same hidden problem of choosing which channel should control a decision, especially when images are vivid but not always semantically decisive. Papers on graph reasoning share the idea that neighbors and relations provide context, while papers on similarity and ranking share the need to score candidates. RMAR sits where those ideas meet: graph structure says what facts can follow, media says what entities look or read like, and relation-aware weighting decides which evidence belongs to this analogy.
303.ww: The mechanism should improve over a fixed fusion baseline because the error it targets is specific: the wrong channel can dominate the answer. If a static system learns that images are often useful, it may keep trusting images even when the query is about an abstract action whose visual signal is weak. RMAR gives the model a way to condition trust on the relation and analogy context. The explicit fingerprint helps before the answer is chosen, by asking whether the induced relation has the right pattern of supporting media. The adaptive gate helps during answer selection, by changing the blend used to score candidate tails. These two paths reduce two different mistakes: inferring the wrong relation from noisy media, and completing the right relation with the wrong evidence mixture. The abstract's ablation claim supports this interpretation: relation-aware modulation is especially effective when modal evidence is weak or ambiguous. That is exactly where a fixed blend has least reason to be trusted.
303.po: The payoff is a more careful analogical reasoner for multimodal knowledge graphs. RMAR can be used with both multimodal knowledge graph representation pipelines and transformer-based pipelines, so the contribution is described as backbone-agnostic rather than tied to one model family. The paper also contributes MCNetAnalogy and MCNetKG, aimed at reducing a benchmark bias toward concrete entities by adding abstract concepts and actions. In experiments, the abstract reports consistent gains across both backbone types and a 29 percent relative improvement on MCNetAnalogy.
303.limits: The claims depend on the modality fingerprint and gates learning reliable evidence patterns from the available data. If the graph, text, or images are sparse, biased, or mismatched to the analogy, the model may learn the wrong trust pattern. The abstract reports gains and ablations, but it does not prove that the learned fingerprints are always interpretable or correct. It also does not show from the abstract alone how RMAR behaves when all modalities are noisy, when relation types are rare, or when a new domain has different rules about which media sources matter.

304.bp: Many Internet of Things devices are small computers with web control panels inside them. A camera, router, sensor hub, or industrial device may expose pages or request handlers that let an owner change settings, read data, restart services, or run maintenance commands. The danger in FalconScope's setting is that some of these interfaces are hidden rather than properly protected. They may not be linked from the visible user interface, but if an attacker discovers the right web request, the device can still answer. The abstract says this can let attackers bypass authentication, alter configurations, leak sensitive data, or execute arbitrary commands. The practical need is therefore a map of what the firmware can secretly respond to, before attackers find those entrances. FalconScope serves device security testing: it tries to enumerate hidden interfaces and confirm unauthorized access by reading how the device routes requests and by creating meaningful HTTP probes.
304.wh: The hard part is that a hidden web interface is not hidden like an unlisted file in a folder. It is often hidden inside firmware logic. A request may need the right path, method, parameter names, header shape, and body format before it reaches the backend handler that performs the action. If a detector only tries many guessed URLs, most guesses never travel through the device's internal routing machinery, so the detector wrongly concludes that no interface exists. That is the false-negative problem named in the abstract. The second difficulty is verification. Even after a possible route is found, the system must send a request that the backend will treat as well formed, then decide whether the response proves unauthorized access. A raw status code or page text may be misleading without understanding what the protocol expects. The paper's tension is completeness versus wasted probing: testing must be broad enough to find hidden routes but precise enough not to drown in invalid requests.
304.naive: A smart beginner would point a web scanner at the device and try a large dictionary of common paths such as admin pages, debug endpoints, configuration URLs, and command names. They might also vary GET and POST requests and look for any unusual response. This fails when the important route identifier is produced or matched by firmware code rather than by visible links or common names. It also fails when the backend handler requires semantically valid parameters before it reveals behavior. Random or template-based requests can miss real handlers because the syntax is wrong, or they can find a response without proving that protected functionality is reachable. The scanner is searching from the outside without knowing the device's own routing rules.
304.ap: FalconScope's central move is to stop treating the device as a black box of guessed web pages. It first inspects the firmware and reconstructs the internal routing mechanism: the code-level rules that connect request identifiers to backend handlers. The abstract calls these Routing Unique Identifiers and their corresponding handlers. That gives the system a candidate map of hidden entrances rather than a bag of guessed URLs. Then FalconScope uses a large language model, meaning a language system used here to interpret and produce structured request text, as a semantic engine. Its job is not to invent vulnerabilities. Its job is to turn route and handler clues into syntactically and semantically valid HTTP requests, then read the device's responses in context. The combination is concrete: static firmware analysis supplies where to probe, and semantic request generation supplies how to probe and how to judge the answer.
304.mech: The mechanism begins with the IoT device firmware, not with live web crawling alone. FalconScope statically analyzes the firmware, meaning it reads the program artifacts without first running every possible request through the device. It looks for the internal routing logic: the places where incoming HTTP requests are matched to identifiers and then dispatched to backend handlers. From that analysis it reconstructs Routing Unique Identifiers and pairs them with the handler code that would run if the right request arrived. This stage produces an enumeration target: a list of likely hidden interfaces that a blind scanner would have to guess. Next, FalconScope prepares probes. For each route or handler, the LLM-powered semantic engine examines the communication clues available from the firmware and constructs HTTP requests with plausible paths, methods, parameters, and content shape. The request must be syntactically valid, so the device parser accepts it, and semantically valid, so the backend logic is actually triggered. FalconScope then sends these probes and observes the device responses. The final validation step interprets those responses semantically rather than merely counting any reply as success. It asks whether the response confirms unauthorized access to the hidden interface. The output is a detected set of hidden web interfaces, grounded in reconstructed routing and confirmed by meaningful request-response behavior.
304.math: The main mathematical idea is program-structure reconstruction. In plain terms, FalconScope treats firmware as a set of paths through instructions: if an incoming request has this identifier, control flows to that handler. Static analysis is a disciplined way of following those paths without trying every possible live input. The object being recovered is like a directed map: request identifiers point to backend handlers. That map matters because security testing becomes a coverage problem, meaning the detector wants to visit as many real handlers as possible while avoiding impossible routes. A second idea is constrained generation. The HTTP request is not just text; it must satisfy constraints imposed by parsers, route matchers, and handler expectations. The LLM is used as a language-based scorer and generator for those constraints, turning clues into requests that are likely to be accepted. A third idea is semantic classification of responses: deciding whether observed output is evidence of unauthorized access. The repeated tradeoff is completeness versus precision. If the route reconstruction is too loose, the system wastes probes and may report noise. If it is too narrow, it misses hidden interfaces. If response interpretation is too trusting, it confuses ordinary errors with access; if too strict, it overlooks real exposures.
304.dots: FalconScope connects to the repo's privacy, federated, and security family through the shared question of what can cross a boundary. Here the boundary is not a training-data boundary or a cryptographic boundary; it is the boundary between a device's intended public web surface and the protected backend functions hidden inside firmware. It also sits near language-model tool-use papers because the LLM is not the whole solution; it is a helper used after a structured source of evidence has been recovered. That differs from papers that ask a language model to reason from text alone. FalconScope first builds a route map from firmware, then asks the model to produce and judge protocol-shaped requests. It also connects to anomaly and vulnerability detection work: the target is a rare, dangerous behavior that ordinary visible browsing will not show. The broader conference pattern is evidence narrowing. Many papers reduce a huge search space by finding structure first; FalconScope does that with firmware routing.
304.ww: FalconScope should work better than blind scanning because it changes the search from guessing names to following the device's own dispatch logic. Hidden interfaces can stay invisible to crawlers because no page links to them, but the firmware still needs rules that tell the device what to do when a matching request arrives. Reconstructing those rules exposes candidates that external probing may never stumble upon. The semantic engine helps with the next failure point: a route is only useful if the request can actually trigger the handler. A request with the wrong parameter names or malformed body may be routed correctly and still do nothing interesting. By generating protocol-aware HTTP requests, FalconScope increases the chance that backend logic is exercised. Semantic validation then reduces the opposite mistake, where a tool sees any response and calls it a vulnerability. The reported results support this intuition: on 11 real-world IoT devices from four major vendors, the abstract says FalconScope detected 620 hidden web interfaces, 103 times more than IoTScope, while using only 3.6% of its analysis time.
304.po: The payoff is a faster and more complete way to uncover hidden attack surfaces in IoT devices. Instead of telling a manufacturer only which visible pages responded to common probes, FalconScope can reveal backend interfaces implied by the firmware's routing logic and confirm whether unauthorized access is possible. The abstract grounds the practical result strongly: evaluation covered 11 real devices from four major vendors, found 620 hidden web interfaces, and led to responsible disclosure in which 50 issues were assigned CVE IDs. The capability bought is not just a better score; it is earlier discovery of exposed device functions that could otherwise remain available to attackers.
304.limits: FalconScope depends on the firmware containing routing logic that static analysis can recover with enough precision. If firmware is encrypted, packed, heavily obfuscated, split across components not available to the analyzer, or dependent on runtime state that static inspection cannot see, the route map may be incomplete or noisy. The LLM-powered engine also depends on clues being sufficient to generate valid HTTP requests and to interpret responses correctly; the abstract does not prove that this will generalize to every vendor protocol or unusual device stack. The evaluation is real but bounded: 11 devices from four vendors. The paper reports detection and disclosure results, but the abstract does not specify false-positive rates, long-term patch outcomes, or behavior on devices with stronger authentication design.

305.bp: This paper serves systems where the thing being watched is not a fixed table but a changing network. A node might be a user, sensor, account, device, or time-series segment. A link says that two things are related in space, time, behavior, or interaction. The practical need is to notice when one part stops fitting the evolving pattern around it: a sensor begins drifting, an account behaves unlike its past neighbors, or a short temporal pattern appears in the wrong context. The abstract frames this as anomaly detection in dynamic graphs. That means the detector must judge abnormality while both the node information and the graph relationships are changing. DyConAD treats the task as a memory and comparison problem. It asks how to preserve important historical features, build time-aware graph structure from shapelets, and score unusual behavior at several scales instead of using one static snapshot of normality.
305.wh: The difficulty is that normal behavior is not a single frozen shape. In a dynamic graph, nodes and relationships evolve, so an event can look strange only when compared with the right time window and the right neighborhood. A detector built for a static graph sees one picture and then tries to decide which nodes differ from that picture. That misses the abstract's central pressure: real-world scenarios contain dynamic information. A second problem appears during updating. As node descriptions change over time, a standard update rule may overwrite old signals or keep new signals without asking which parts are important. If it forgets too much, it loses the baseline needed to recognize a meaningful departure. If it remembers everything equally, noise and stale facts can crowd out useful evidence. The detector needs to keep selected history, track temporal structure, and still produce an anomaly score efficiently.
305.naive: A smart beginner would take each graph snapshot, run a normal graph anomaly detector on it, and flag nodes whose current features or links look far from the majority. Another beginner version would update each node's representation at every time step by mixing the new observation into the old one. Both choices are too blunt. Snapshot detection ignores the path that led to the current graph, so gradual drift and sudden breaks can be confused. Uniform updating assumes every new feature deserves the same memory and every old feature deserves the same decay. That fails when important earlier patterns should be protected, or when recent noise should not rewrite the model's idea of normal behavior.
305.ap: The paper's core move is to turn dynamic graph anomaly detection into two coordinated channels of comparison. One channel strengthens memory: as node representations evolve, the model tries to selectively preserve features that remain important for judging future behavior. The other channel scores abnormality through similarity at multiple scales, meaning it does not ask only whether the present node is unlike one fixed reference. It asks how the node compares across different temporal or structural views of the evolving graph. DyConAD also builds the dynamic graph itself from time-aware shapelets. A shapelet is a short temporal pattern, such as a small rise-fall pattern in a sensor trace, that can stand for a recurring local behavior. By extracting these time-aware pieces and establishing spatiotemporal relationships between them, the method gives the graph structure a direct connection to how patterns unfold over time.
305.mech: The mechanism starts with temporal data that can be organized as a dynamic graph. The input contains nodes with information changing over time, plus enough temporal signal to extract shapelets. First, the dynamic graph construction step looks for time-aware shapelets: short segments whose shape carries useful evidence about local temporal behavior. Instead of treating raw time points as isolated numbers, it uses these segments as meaningful units and establishes spatiotemporal relationships between them, so the graph records both when patterns occur and how they relate across space or structure. Next, DyConAD updates node representations over time. A representation here is a compact description of a node's observed features and graph context. The memory enhancement strategy decides which parts of the evolving description should be retained rather than overwritten. Then the detector forms anomaly evidence through multi-scale similarity-based scoring. At each chosen scale, it compares the current pattern with relevant stored or neighboring patterns and asks how well it fits. A small mismatch at one scale may be ordinary noise; a mismatch that persists across temporal or structural scales is stronger evidence. The output is an anomaly score for graph elements, grounded in changing structure, remembered history, and similarity across several views.
305.math: The main mathematical object is a dynamic graph: nodes are the entities or temporal pattern units, links express spatiotemporal relationships, and both node information and relationships can change. The first idea is graph reasoning, which means letting connected objects carry evidence for one another, but only after deciding what the links mean. Here links are useful because an abnormal node or shapelet is judged partly by its relationship to other time-aware patterns. The second idea is similarity. Similarity compresses many differences into a score: two shapelets or node states are close if their temporal shape, graph context, or learned description matches in the way the detector considers relevant. The third idea is memory under selective update. Mathematically, an update rule chooses how much old information and new information remain in the current state. DyConAD's memory enhancement exists because equal retention is a poor rule when some features are important warnings and others are noise. The fourth idea is multi-scale scoring. A scale is a chosen level of detail, such as short versus longer temporal behavior or local versus broader graph context. The tradeoff is sensitivity versus false alarms: compare too narrowly and noise looks suspicious; compare too broadly and brief but real anomalies disappear.
305.dots: This paper connects directly to the fraud and anomaly family because it repairs a weak definition of normal. Normal is not just the majority pattern in one graph; it is a moving pattern that must be remembered, compared, and updated. It also belongs to graph learning because the answer depends on relationships among nodes or shapelets, not on one record alone. The time-series and spatiotemporal family is present through shapelets: short temporal patterns become building blocks for graph construction, so order and timing are part of the evidence. The recurring conference idea is measured surprise. DyConAD measures surprise by comparing current behavior with remembered and multi-scale graph-temporal evidence. Neighboring papers on scalable graph anomaly detection, time-series anomaly detection, and dynamic graph retrieval share the same pressure: more data is not enough unless the system knows which past pattern, neighbor, or scale deserves trust.
305.ww: The approach should work better than the naive one because it gives the detector a more faithful baseline. An anomaly is meaningful only relative to a notion of expected behavior. Static graph methods build that expectation from one graph state, so they can miss changes that unfold over time. DyConAD's memory enhancement keeps selected historical features available, allowing a node's present state to be judged against more than the latest noisy observation. The shapelet construction helps because short temporal shapes can capture reusable local behaviors more cleanly than individual timestamps. A repeated small pattern can be compared across the graph even when absolute values differ. Multi-scale similarity scoring adds another safeguard. Some abnormal events are sharp and local; others are slow and visible only across a longer window or broader structural context. Looking at several scales reduces dependence on a single fragile comparison. The method therefore improves by aligning the detector's evidence with the actual structure of the problem: changing nodes, changing relations, remembered history, and repeated temporal shapes.
305.po: The payoff is a dynamic graph anomaly detector that explicitly handles time-varying information instead of forcing real-world streams into a static graph assumption. The abstract reports experiments on four real-world datasets and three public datasets from the UCR Time Series Archive, with improvements over existing approaches in detection accuracy and efficiency. In practical terms, the method buys more reliable warning signals for systems where abnormal behavior is partly temporal and partly relational. It can use shapelets to build time-aware graph structure, memory to avoid careless forgetting, and multi-scale similarity scores to flag deviations that a single snapshot detector may miss.
305.limits: The abstract does not specify the exact memory rule, the scales used for similarity scoring, or which graph elements receive final anomaly scores, so those details cannot be reconstructed beyond the stated design. The method assumes that useful shapelets can be extracted and that their spatiotemporal relationships reflect real structure rather than noise. It also assumes important features can be selectively preserved during updates. If anomalies do not resemble shapelet-level departures, if graph links are misleading, or if normal behavior changes faster than memory can adapt, the detector may fail. Reported dataset gains do not by themselves prove reliability under new domains, adversaries, or severe drift.

306.bp: Epidemiologists, social scientists, and engineers need to simulate how diseases spread, how information propagates through social networks, and how opinions evolve in populations. These simulations help predict outcomes and guide policy. But real-world networks have billions of nodes and edges, and standard simulators are far too slow to handle them.
306.wh: Naive simulation updates each node one at a time, checking all its neighbors every step—this is crushingly slow on large graphs. Distributed computing helps, but unless you're careful about how you split the graph, nodes will send constant messages between machines, creating a communication bottleneck that kills the speedup.
306.ap: FS_GPlib uses a two-level acceleration strategy. At the fine level, it synchronizes message-passing updates across multiple nodes at once, using optimized tensor operations that run fast on modern hardware. At the coarse level, it batches many Monte Carlo simulations (random sample-based estimates of propagation) together. To distribute across machines, it partitions the graph not randomly but in a clever way based on the nodes you care about predicting, minimizing cross-machine messages.
306.ww: Batching updates and using tensor hardware (GPUs/TPUs) multiplies throughput without changing the algorithm's correctness. Intelligent graph partitioning keeps nodes that communicate frequently on the same machine, so most message-passing stays local. Monte Carlo batching lets you run thousands of propagation scenarios in parallel.
306.po: The library achieves up to 35,000-fold speedups over standard tools and can simulate a billion-edge graph in 11 seconds while maintaining accuracy. It supports 29 propagation models (epidemics, opinion dynamics, spreading on networks), making it practical for real-world policy analysis.

307.bp: Social networks have legitimate users and bad actors (bots, scammers, coordinated abuse) who pose real security and privacy risks. Detecting abnormal users is critical but hard because you often have very few examples of known abusers to learn from. When you do have labels, they come from expensive manual review.
307.wh: Most graph-based detection methods correlate features (user follows suspicious accounts, posts at odd hours) but don't distinguish signal from noise. A genuine spike in posting at 3 AM could be a night-shift worker or a bot farm—correlation alone can't tell. Moreover, with only a handful of labeled abnormal users, the detector might memorize those specific examples rather than learning generalizable patterns.
307.ap: CIFAD uses a sparse lagged attention encoder to model temporal relationships between different types of edges in the social network (follow, like, message, etc.) at different time lags. It then applies causal-invariant subspace decomposition, which is a mathematical technique for separating the data into two parts: stable causal signals (the real malicious behavior) and dynamic noise (random fluctuations in normal behavior). Finally, it uses influence functions and coverage optimization to decide which unlabeled users should be manually reviewed to maximize the learning from limited labeling budget.
307.ww: By decomposing into causal and noise components, the detector learns patterns robust to random fluctuation in normal user behavior. Influence functions identify the most informative users to label—those whose labels would most improve the model. This active selection makes efficient use of scarce labeled data.
307.po: The method detects anomalous users more accurately than baselines, even in the few-shot regime where you have very few known examples. By learning causal patterns rather than correlations, it generalizes better to new types of attacks not seen during training.

308.bp: Real-world decisions often involve choosing between conflicting moral principles: should a hospital prioritize saving lives (utilitarian) or respect patients' explicit wishes even if it means worse outcomes (deontological)? The multi-armed bandit framework lets machines learn which actions work well, but it doesn't account for this fundamental moral conflict—different stakeholders have different values.
308.wh: A standard bandit algorithm tries to maximize a single reward signal, assuming everyone agrees on what 'good' means. But when multiple ethical frameworks are defensible, there is no universally correct reward. Ignoring moral uncertainty means imposing one framework silently and excluding legitimate values.
308.ap: This paper extends the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm, a standard bandit method, by adding dynamic moral weights. Each ethical framework (utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics) gets a weight that reflects how much that framework should influence the decision. As the algorithm learns by observing outcomes, it updates these weights, allowing the decision-maker to gradually favor frameworks that are working better in practice.
308.ww: By making moral weights explicit and adaptive, the system remains transparent about value trade-offs. The algorithm can learn which frameworks perform better empirically while respecting that multiple viewpoints are legitimate. The UCB approach ensures the algorithm explores different ethical perspectives before exploiting the most promising one.
308.po: The framework balances ethical considerations with performance—it doesn't maximize outcomes at the expense of values, nor does it paralyze decision-making by treating all frameworks as forever equal. It offers a flexible tool for applications like resource allocation, hiring, and content moderation where moral uncertainty is unavoidable.

309.bp: When a search engine retrieves documents in response to a query, it ranks them by relevance. To make ranking better, you can summarize documents so the ranker focuses on the most important parts. But here's the catch: the ranker was trained to score full documents, not summaries. A summary-based ranker may rank very differently, harming performance in production.
309.wh: A simple approach is to train a summarizer on linguistic quality (is it clear and correct?) and a ranker on document relevance, separately. But these solve different problems: a well-written summary might miss information the ranker needs, and the ranker's notion of relevance assumes full documents. When they're decoupled, there's a mismatch—the ranker's weights were optimized for one input distribution but receive a different one at test time.
309.ap: ReSuMe uses reinforcement learning to optimize both the summarizer and ranker jointly. It first trains a language model to generate summaries, then uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to fine-tune it using retrieval relevance (how much does this summary help the ranker?) rather than linguistic quality. In parallel, it updates the retriever model using the generated summaries as training data, so the ranker learns to work with the summaries it will actually receive.
309.ww: By alternating between improving the summarizer (based on ranker feedback) and improving the ranker (based on the summaries it gets), the two components co-adapt. The summarizer learns to preserve information the ranker values, and the ranker learns to exploit the structure of these summaries. The reinforcement learning approach avoids the distribution shift problem.
309.po: Results show substantial improvements: 13.2% better ranking at top-10 and 6.7% better recall at top-100 compared to baselines. The framework produces a high-quality summarizer as a side benefit, and because it's model-agnostic, it can boost any retrieval system.

310.bp: Online e-commerce platforms like Amazon and Alibaba use automated agents to decide how much merchants should bid on keywords and how much discount to offer on products. These decisions directly drive revenue for the platform and merchants. The challenge is that decisions on bidding and discounting are intertwined—increasing a bid attracts more clicks, but discounting can increase conversion, and both are limited by the merchant's budget.
310.wh: Naive approaches treat bidding and discounting separately or rely on hand-crafted rules ('if clicks are low, increase bid'). This misses the complex interplay: a high bid + low discount might waste the budget on clicks that don't convert, while a low bid + high discount might give away profit on the few clicks you get. Moreover, on dynamic platforms, the merchants' goals and budget constraints change constantly.
310.ap: GAM uses a pre-trained language model as the backbone and trains it end-to-end via reinforcement learning (Group Relative Policy Optimization). The model jointly decides bidding and coupon discounting in sequence, treating it as a sequential decision problem. It includes a constraint-aware reward module that ensures the self-funding constraint is respected: the budget for both actions must come from the agent's commission revenue, not an external budget.
310.ww: Language models are naturally good at sequential reasoning and following instructions, so they can learn complex interdependencies between bidding and discounting. By training with reinforcement learning on real business metrics (revenue, profit, budget), the model learns policies that actually work in the real world. The constraint-aware module prevents the agent from making unrealistic decisions.
310.po: On a large real-world offline environment, the framework balances revenue maximization with constraint satisfaction, outperforming rule-based and standard RL baselines. It provides a general, learnable alternative to hardcoded bidding strategies.

311.bp: Web companies collect massive datasets of user behavior, product interactions, and transactions—billions of rows with hundreds of features each. Predicting outcomes (will this user buy, will this transaction be fraud, will this system fail?) from tabular data is a fundamental problem. The challenge is that these features are messy: some are wildly heavy-tailed (a few giant values, many tiny ones), some change over time, and relationships between features are complex and nonlinear.
311.wh: Standard gradient boosting (tree-based models) struggles with heavy-tailed and anisotropic features because trees are designed for simpler, more uniform data. Deep learning models help but require manual feature engineering—a human expert must carefully transform raw features into useful forms, which is slow, error-prone, and doesn't generalize to new datasets.
311.ap: KMLP is a hybrid architecture combining two components. A Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) sits in front and learns nonlinear transformations for each feature independently, using learnable activation functions to automatically adapt to each feature's distribution and nonlinearity. Behind that, a gated multilayer perceptron (gMLP) learns relationships and interactions between the transformed features. This two-stage design automates feature engineering while capturing high-order feature interactions.
311.ww: KANs have learnable activation functions that can bend and adapt to any input distribution, so they naturally handle heavy-tailed and anisotropic features without manual scaling. By putting the KAN stage first, each feature gets personalized treatment. The gMLP stage then focuses on learning clean interactions from the refined features, rather than fighting with raw feature distributions.
311.po: On public benchmarks and a massive industrial dataset with billions of samples, KMLP matches or beats gradient boosting while eliminating manual feature engineering. The combination avoids the training efficiency bottlenecks of standard deep learning while capturing the same nonlinear relationships.

312.bp: Machine learning companies offer prediction services over the web (image recognition, medical diagnosis) but users want privacy—they don't want to send raw data to the server. Secure multi-party computation enables a server and user to jointly compute a prediction without the server ever seeing the raw input data, but it's slow and communication-intensive, especially for large models like vision transformers.
312.wh: Vision transformers use attention mechanisms that create highly correlated computations across layers and positions—information needs to flow between distant parts of the model. Naive approaches to secure computation treat each layer the same, not realizing that some layers are communication-heavy while others are compute-heavy. Different layers and positions have different privacy-efficiency trade-offs.
312.ap: SecViT redesigns vision transformers specifically for secure multi-party computation. It analyzes each layer and each position in the model and adapts the attention mechanism to minimize communication under privacy constraints. It adds a 'layer-dependent and load-balancing' attention adapter that reuses features across correlated layers, and develops approximation algorithms for expensive attention and activation operations that preserve accuracy while cutting communication.
312.ww: By analyzing which computations are expensive in the secure setting (communication-heavy), the system can selectively approximate them without harming results. Reusing features across correlated layers reduces redundant secure computation. These optimizations exploit the specific structure of vision transformers rather than applying generic CNN optimizations.
312.po: SecViT reduces communication by 6x and latency by 4.6x compared to prior work while maintaining the same accuracy. This makes private inference over transformers practical for real-world scenarios where users want both privacy and fast predictions.

313.bp: Knowledge is often represented as formal logic rules in ontologies (like OWL, a semantic web standard). To reason over this knowledge, a system must generate proofs—step-by-step logical explanations of why a conclusion follows from the rules. When humans read a proof, they want to understand not just that something is true, but why. Large language models are trained to generate text, but can they generate valid, human-readable logical proofs?
313.wh: Generating proofs is harder than answering questions because a proof must be logically sound (each step must follow from previous premises) and complete (cover all necessary steps). Most work on LLMs focuses on simple reasoning tasks where the model just predicts an answer, not on explaining how it arrived at that answer with formal justification. Logical complexity and formal notation both make this task difficult.
313.ap: This paper builds a dataset and evaluation framework for proof generation in OWL ontologies. It breaks proof generation into sub-tasks: Extraction (find relevant rules), Simplification (make rules easier to understand), and Explanation (convert to natural language). It evaluates a dozen LLMs on these tasks and measures logical completeness (do the proofs actually prove the claim?).
313.ww: By decomposing proof generation into stages, you can identify where models fail. Logical complexity—not fancy notation—is the real blocker: models handle simple chains of reasoning but break on complex proofs. Understanding where models struggle helps identify what makes formal reasoning hard.
313.po: The paper reveals that some models produce strong overall results but fail on complex proofs, that logical structure matters more than notation format, and that noise in input data severely hurts performance. This grounds expectations for what LLMs can and can't do for formal verification and knowledge reasoning tasks.

314.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products, movies, or songs to users based on their past behavior. In practice, popular items (bestsellers, blockbusters) are recommended frequently while niche items rarely appear, even if some users would love them. This 'long-tail' problem means niche item sales and user satisfaction suffer. Large language models are being used as recommenders, but they inherit the same long-tail bias from their training data.
314.wh: An LLM trained on web text and user behavior data has seen millions of mentions of 'Harry Potter' but few mentions of obscure indie films. When recommending, it naturally defaults to the popular items it knows well. Users interested in niche items get frustrated. Naive fine-tuning doesn't fix this because the bias comes partly from the pretraining data (implicit prior) and partly from the recommendation dataset itself (data long-tail).
314.ap: EISAM applies Sharpness-Aware Minimization, a technique from optimization, at the item level. During training, it computes a penalty for each item based on how sharp (locally unstable) the loss landscape is around that item's predictions. Unpopular items tend to have sharper loss landscapes because of limited training examples. EISAM increases the penalty for sharp-loss items, forcing the model to find solutions that work reliably for tail items too.
314.ww: Sharpness in the loss landscape means the model's predictions are fragile—small changes in weights make large changes in recommendations. Tail items, with few training examples, naturally have sharp loss landscapes. By penalizing sharpness, the model learns to be more robust and generalize better to unseen tail items. The item-level design captures fine-grained differences in how popular each item is.
314.po: The method improves recommendation quality for tail items while maintaining head-item performance, and includes a theoretical analysis showing the generalization bound improves faster with the method. This addresses the long-standing practical problem in e-commerce where recommenders systematically ignore niche catalog items.
